title: Golden Dome Is Technologically and Financially Infeasible
gist: APS physicists Frederick Lamb and Laura Grego argue Golden Dome cannot defeat even a limited nuclear ballistic missile attack within 15 years, especially its space-based boost-phase interceptors, which would need tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of satellites. They cite a CBO estimate of about $1.2 trillion as a likely substantial underestimate and urge canceling the space interceptor program in favor of arms control.

themes.theme: Track record and scale of the threat

insights.claim: The US has spent more than $500 billion (2025 dollars) over seven decades on missile defenses, yet no system has demonstrated an ability to intercept even a single missile or warhead under expected nuclear-attack conditions.
insights.speaker: Frederick Lamb and Laura Grego
insights.so_what: A weak track record cautions against pricing Golden Dome as a proven program.

insights.claim: No missile defense capable of defeating a major Russian or Chinese attack of hundreds or thousands of warheads with decoys and countermeasures is foreseeable, and there is no prospect within 15 years of reliably defending even against a limited coercive raid.
insights.speaker: Frederick Lamb and Laura Grego
insights.so_what: Expect Golden Dome capability claims to fall short of its stated scope; arms control remains the real risk reducer.

insights.claim: A smaller threat set includes North Korea possibly launching 20 ICBMs with multiple warheads, an unauthorized Russian submarine launch of 16 missiles carrying about 100 warheads, and a limited coercive strike of a dozen missiles with 60 warheads.
insights.speaker: Frederick Lamb and Laura Grego
insights.so_what: Defines the sizing baseline against which defense architectures should be judged.

insights.claim: Even with planned improvements, the ground-based midcourse defense is not expected to provide robust defense against more than a few missiles with simple countermeasures for 15 years; its tests were scripted for success and it has not solved decoy discrimination.
insights.speaker: Frederick Lamb and Laura Grego
insights.so_what: Existing GMD upgrades will not deliver Golden Dome's headline promise.

insights.claim: THAAD and Aegis SM-3 Block IIA were designed for regional defense, not ICBMs, and upgrading and testing them for the strategic role would take a decade or more; the Middle East war showed that even firing several interceptors at each medium-range missile does not guarantee interception.
insights.speaker: Frederick Lamb and Laura Grego
insights.so_what: Interceptor consumption rates and costs limit scaling of terminal systems.

insights.claim: Space Force General Michael Guetlein, who leads Golden Dome, has advocated directed-energy weapons to cut costs, but weapons with required power, tracking and durability would take decades if feasible.
insights.speaker: Frederick Lamb and Laura Grego
insights.so_what: Directed-energy cost relief is long-dated; do not expect near-term revenue pools.

themes.theme: Boost-phase physics and the space interceptor problem

insights.claim: Boost-phase intercept is constrained by time: modern ICBMs burn for about three minutes or less, a defender cannot confidently fire until at least 75 seconds after launch, leaving 45 to 75 seconds for interception and decision times of tens of seconds, raising accidental-escalation risk.
insights.speaker: Frederick Lamb and Laura Grego
insights.so_what: Compressed timelines undermine human-in-the-loop control and add crisis instability.
insights.locator: Boost-Phase Intercept and the Tyranny of Time

insights.claim: North Korea's Hwasong-18 burns about 170 seconds but needs only about 158 seconds to hit Seattle and 137 seconds for Fairbanks, and Russia's RS-24 Yars needs about 150 seconds for Seattle or Boston.
insights.speaker: Frederick Lamb and Laura Grego
insights.so_what: Real missiles already leave little margin for boost-phase intercept.
insights.locator: Boost-Phase Intercept and the Tyranny of Time

insights.claim: Building a boost-phase defense would incentivize adversaries to deploy fast-burn missiles, closer launch sites and depressed trajectories, a classic 'fallacy of the last move'; a 1985 OTA report found an MX-sized ICBM could burn out in under 60 seconds.
insights.speaker: Frederick Lamb and Laura Grego
insights.so_what: Countermeasure response cheaply erodes the value of expensive defenses.
insights.locator: Boost-Phase Intercept and the Tyranny of Time

insights.claim: Because orbiting interceptors are rarely where needed, defending the lower 48 against four ICBMs from one area needs about 24,000 interceptors, a salvo of 10 needs at least 60,000, and firing three at each target would need 180,000.
insights.speaker: Frederick Lamb and Laura Grego
insights.so_what: Constellation size implies launch and manufacturing volumes far beyond current capacity and budgets.
insights.locator: Space-Based Intercept Would Require Enormous Numbers of Interceptors

insights.claim: In the Iran conflict, Israel and the US fired two to five interceptors at each incoming missile, and Ukraine fired two to four until supply ran low, after which firing only one let many Russian missiles through.
insights.speaker: Frederick Lamb and Laura Grego
insights.so_what: Interceptor inventory and cost-exchange ratios are decisive; demand for interceptor production persists.
insights.locator: Space-Based Intercept Would Require Enormous Numbers of Interceptors

insights.claim: Faster 10 km/s interceptors could cut the required number but would be tens of times more massive and costly, and the smaller constellation would be more vulnerable to attack.
insights.speaker: Frederick Lamb and Laura Grego
insights.so_what: No cheap architecture escapes the cost-vs-vulnerability tradeoff.
insights.locator: Space-Based Intercept Would Require Enormous Numbers of Interceptors

insights.claim: A recent CBO report estimated the strategic missile defense component of Golden Dome at about $1.2 trillion, but the authors say it assessed a limited system and its 7,800-interceptor figure rests on unrealistic assumptions, so a robust space layer would cost trillions over 20 years.
insights.speaker: Frederick Lamb and Laura Grego
insights.so_what: Official cost estimates may be materially understated; budget fights and scope cuts are likely.
insights.locator: Space-Based Intercept Would Require Enormous Numbers of Interceptors

insights.claim: Space-based interceptor prototypes are slated for flight demonstrations in 2027 and integration into Golden Dome by 2028, with contracts worth up to $3.2 billion for on-orbit tests by 2028 awarded to 12 firms.
insights.speaker: Frederick Lamb and Laura Grego
insights.so_what: The 2027 to 2028 demonstrations are the key milestones for contractors; the authors urge cancellation.
insights.locator: Boost-Phase Intercept and the Tyranny of Time

insights.claim: Adversaries can defeat boost-phase defense with salvos, multiple reentry vehicles with their own motors such as Russia's developing Yars-M, rocket-propelled decoys, anti-satellite attacks and nuclear detonations in space.
insights.speaker: Frederick Lamb and Laura Grego
insights.so_what: Offense is cheaper than defense, so the cost-exchange ratio favors attackers.
insights.locator: How Countermeasures Can Make a Boost-Phase Defense Fail

insights.claim: The authors recommend canceling the space-based interceptor program now, shifting resources to risk reduction and arms control, and note the 2012 National Research Council conclusion against investing in boost-phase defense remains valid.
insights.speaker: Frederick Lamb and Laura Grego
insights.so_what: Policy risk to space interceptor contractors if the critique gains traction in Congress.
